name: Rice bran extract

lead: Rice bran extract comes from the outer layer of milled rice and appears in Asian skincare for brightening, hydration and antioxidant effects, giving brighter, smoother skin. Rice bran and rice water have a long history of traditional use.

Constituents such as ferulic acid, gamma-oryzanol, tocopherols and, in pigmented rice, anthocyanins act as antioxidants in test systems. In melanoma cells a fermented extract lowered MITF, a regulator of melanin production, and reduced melanin-pathway signalling in mouse cells. Controlled human trials for skin tone were not found.

paras: It is used in essences, serums, creams and cleansers, often fermented, as part of a daily brightening and moisturizing routine.
Safety assessments summarized by Grokipedia describe low irritation potential at typical cosmetic concentrations; that summary was not independently verified.

angle.text: Popular in K-beauty and J-beauty products for brightening, moisturizing and antioxidant effects, for less dullness and smoother skin. Lab studies show antioxidant activity and reduced melanin signalling in mouse cells.

lead: Rice bran extract is a cosmetic ingredient derived from the bran layer of rice (Oryza sativa), a by-product of milling. It is used in skincare, especially K-beauty and J-beauty products, for brightening, moisturizing and antioxidant effects [1].

Laboratory studies show that rice bran extracts contain antioxidants such as phenolic acids, anthocyanins (in pigmented rice), tocopherol and gamma-oryzanol [2][3], and that a fermented extract reduced melanin-related signaling in mouse melanoma cells [4]. The sources reviewed contain no controlled human trial of topical rice bran extract for skin tone; the Grokipedia article describes clinical results, but it is AI-generated and its citations were not independently verified here.
infobox: Ferulic acid, gamma-oryzanol, phytic acid, tocopherols, anthocyanins in pigmented rice [1][2]
Plain and fermented extracts; powder (nuka) and rice water in traditional use [1]

paras: Rice bran is the outer layer removed when brown rice is polished into white rice, making up roughly 8 to 10 percent of the paddy weight, according to Grokipedia [1]. It spoils quickly because of lipase activity, so it is stabilized, often by heat, before extraction [1].

Grokipedia reports that rice-washing water and rice bran powder (nuka) have been used for skin and hair care in Japan, China and elsewhere in Asia, with Japanese use said to date to the Heian period; it also describes a belief that sake brewers' hands stayed smooth and pale from handling rice [1]. These historical accounts come from an AI-generated source and were not checked against primary sources.
Modern formulations, including fermented extracts, feature in K-beauty and J-beauty lines [1].

Analyses of pigmented (black and red) rice brans found higher reducing power than a white rice bran extract, and the extracts inhibited lipid peroxidation in test systems [2]. Studies of Thai rice bran varieties likewise measured phenolic, flavonoid, tocopherol and gamma-oryzanol content and antioxidant activity in vitro [5].

In B16F1 mouse melanoma cells, fermented rice bran downregulated MITF expression and inhibited melanogenesis induced by alpha-MSH [4]. Black rice bran also reduced chemically induced inflammation in mouse skin [6].
No controlled human studies of topical rice bran extract for skin brightening were found in the PubMed material reviewed. The research above is laboratory and animal work.

Grokipedia reports that human studies of rice-derived formulations measured improved hydration and that a 10 percent black rice bran lotion reduced melanin and erythema within 14 days [1]; these statements were not verified against the original trials. Registered human trials of oral rice bran extract address immunity, depression and pharmacokinetics rather than skin [7][8].
Grokipedia states that rice-derived cosmetic ingredients are generally considered to have low potential for irritation, allergenicity and phototoxicity in safety assessments [1].
